claims.text: High-energy ball milling followed by optimized spark-plasma sintering will produce a W–Cu composite with significantly reduced void fraction and improved interfacial contact.
Reduced void fraction and improved interfacial contact will result in higher thermal conductivity and mechanical durability than conventional infiltration or powder sintering.
The starting W and Cu powders will have particle sizes below 10 μm.
High-energy ball milling will achieve nanostructured mixing of the W and Cu powders.
SPS will be conducted under inert gas or vacuum using a temperature ramp below the Cu boiling point, above the Cu melting point, and below the W melting point.
The SPS processing window is 900–1100 °C, 50–100 MPa, and a dwell time of 5–30 minutes in an inert atmosphere.
The composite is intended to withstand thermal cycling and neutron irradiation representative of fusion-reactor joint conditions.
The intervention will create a nanostructured W–Cu interface with minimal voids and high interfacial contact area.
Mechanical alloying breaks up oxide films.
Mechanical alloying promotes intimate mixing of W and Cu.
Rapid SPS consolidation minimizes grain growth and void formation.
The resulting dense composite will contain enhanced thermal pathways and have greater mechanical strength.
The ball-milled and SPS-processed material will have at least 20% higher thermal conductivity than infiltrated or conventionally sintered W–Cu baselines.
The ball-milled and SPS-processed material will have at least 20% higher mechanical durability, including flexural strength or toughness, than the stated baselines.
The ball-milled and SPS-processed material will have a void fraction below 2%.
The magnitude of improvement depends on powder quality, milling parameters, and SPS optimization.
Grain refinement may trade off against mechanical toughness.

contradictions.description: The intervention requires SPS above the Cu melting point, but the stated 900–1100 °C window includes temperatures well below Cu's melting point; only the upper end is above melting.

The predicted outcome treats void fraction below 2% as success, whereas the falsification rule literally says the hypothesis is falsified if the void fraction is below 2%. The rule likely intended to say that failure to reach below 2% is falsifying.
